topics.label: Deep-pipe root-zone irrigation
topics.description: Water is poured into a pipe placed beside a transplant so it enters below the evaporating soil surface. In the Sonoran mesquite experiment an open-ended 5 cm diameter pipe had its base 50 cm deep and a reported volume of 2 L. It is a delivery conduit; its nominal internal volume is not proof of slow release or long-term storage. Soil infiltration and the depth of the roots determine where water goes. Keep this general method separate from LIFE NIEBLAS’s project-specific traditional pipe-watering treatment and from the soil-filled Irrigasc sleeve.

topics.label: Study: Sonoran mesquite irrigation and mulch (1995–1999)
topics.description: Bainbridge and colleagues tested establishment of 144 nursery-grown honey mesquite seedlings at an abandoned Sonoran Desert borrow pit. Eight blocks compared deep-pipe, buried-clay-pot and surface irrigation, crossed with bark mulch, vertical stem mulch and bare ground. Two seedlings occupied each plot, and tree shelters protected plants. Planted on 16 November 1995 and assessed on 21 June 1999, deep-pipe plants had 71% survival, clay-pot plants 52%, and surface-watered plants 23%; water inputs were comparable across treatments. Neither mulch treatment significantly improved survival or growth. Irrigation changed over establishment and totalled less than 20 L per plant over 3.5 years. Herbivory affected growth and there was no contemporaneous no-water control. Published in 2001, this is field evidence for delivery method in a specific species, soil and climate, without drone delivery or validation of a half-litre frequent-refill schedule.

topics.label: Study: Nodriza reservoir establishment trials (2012–2014)
topics.description: Torres and colleagues report two field experiments evaluating the integrated Nodriza reservoir, ceramic outlet and protective shelter for two-year-old Quercus rotundifolia nursery stock grown in approximately 300 cm³ forest trays. Experiment A at Las Hazas compared Nodriza with controls in 2012–2013; Experiment B near Bailén compared Nodriza, Groasis and controls in 2013–2014. The paper reports improved moisture conditions and several growth responses, but its survival observations require care: Experiment A had complete separation and an uninformative GLM, while Experiment B’s survival difference was not statistically significant. Device and shelter effects cannot be independently attributed. Initial watering and summer refills differed between experiments, so they are not a single transferable dose schedule. Published on 11 September 2026, the study supplies historical component and establishment evidence; long-term durability, lifecycle costs and formal cost-effectiveness remain untested, as does any drone refill interface.

topics.label: Trial A: Nodriza at Las Hazas (2012–2013)
topics.description: Experiment A followed Quercus rotundifolia seedlings at Las Hazas from March 2012 to April 2013, comparing 30 Nodriza plants with 11 controls. Methods describe 35 L initial watering and a July 35 L watering, which must be retained alongside the abstract’s description of non-irrigated controls; the exact control-water treatment needs reconciliation. Observed survival was 86.7% with Nodriza and zero in controls. However, Results explicitly report GLM p = 0.99 and complete separation caused by all controls dying, preventing a reliable statistical inference of treatment differences. Moisture and growth observations remain source-scoped. The integrated shelter/reservoir treatment and unequal sample sizes limit attribution and transfer. This completed historical experiment, published in 2026, does not establish guaranteed survival, a minimum irrigation dose, or the effectiveness of drone servicing.

topics.label: Trial B: Nodriza and Groasis at Bailén (2013–2014)
topics.description: Experiment B ran from February 2013 to February 2014 near Bailén with 15 Nodriza plants, 15 Groasis plants and 10 controls, using two-year-old Quercus rotundifolia stock. Devices were filled at installation and controls received 30 L; the wet spring supplied 289.8 mm rainfall and no additional dry-season refilling was performed. The observed survival proportions were 100%, 87% and 70% respectively, but the reported survival GLM found no significant difference (p = 0.608). Moisture and some growth responses differed, without independently isolating the reservoir from protective shelter effects. This historical field comparison, published in 2026, therefore informs context-dependent establishment performance and servicing questions. It does not prove a statistically reliable survival advantage, validate a universal summer refill interval, or test aerial water transfer.

topics.label: Study: Dubai individual-plant drone watering prototype (2026)
topics.description: Antony Sheshenya’s Dubai American Academy study built a removable pump and tank for a Mavic 2 Pro and a wireless soil-probe link, tested around six potted basil plants in a covered courtyard. Eight bench runs measured pump flow, followed by ground tests, nine loaded flights and six integrated sensor-controlled flights. The aircraft was manually piloted; the pump used an uncalibrated relative moisture index with hysteresis. Integrated-flight water quantities were estimated from bench flow multiplied by pump-on time, not collected at the plant. The study demonstrates preliminary payload/control feasibility but did not measure targeting accuracy, root-zone capture fraction, routine safe payload, useful endurance or plant benefit. It calls for a rated airframe and further testing. Publisher HTML is dated 3 November 2026, while the PDF lists electronic access on 15 November 2026; that unresolved date discrepancy is preserved. No autonomous flight or reservoir-filling result is established.

topics.label: Proposed drone-refilled seedling reservoir
topics.description: User proposal from the 10 November 2026 chat: plant nursery stock together with a tube or local reservoir, then have a drone visit and refill it. The suggested 0.5 L every couple of days is an assumed design scenario; species, soil, climate, stock size and exact interval are unspecified. Reviewed sources establish separate components: buried pipe/sleeve delivery, passive reservoirs, small manually piloted water-payload tests, an indoor funnel invention, and larger agricultural spray aircraft. Their combination has not been validated in the reviewed evidence. A fill opening, transferred-volume measurement, overflow/loss control and a suitable soil outlet must work together. As a capacity-only calculation, 40 L divided by an assumed 0.5 L gives 80 fills before reserves, losses, travel and time constraints; it is not measured plants per flight or per hour. topics.label: Study: Bingham Canyon Waterboxx establishment (2020–2022)
topics.description: Lund and colleagues compared Waterboxx with controls for five woody taxa on semiarid mine overburden in Utah. Ten split blocks contained 400 seedlings in pairs, planted in November 2020 or May 2021 and followed through June 2022. Responses depended on species and season: spring Cercocarpus survival was 30% in controls versus 65% with devices; autumn Pinus edulis was 35% versus 75%. Atriplex survival was high without a detectable device benefit. All seedlings received 3 L initially and each device additionally received 15 L, so device effects and added initial water cannot be separated. Published in 2024, this historical field study is represented from partial primary-publisher excerpts; direct PDF acquisition and supplementary material remain unavailable. It tested establishment, not drone servicing.

topics.label: Small-reservoir refill access
topics.description: Refill access is the opening and servicing arrangement used to add water to a local planting reservoir. The reviewed Groasis sheets describe a siphon in Growboxx and a capped cover opening in Waterboxx. These features establish that additional filling is contemplated, but give no tested autonomous aircraft connection, opening diameter, docking tolerance, automatic cap handling or spill-control protocol. An aerial refill concept therefore needs an independently demonstrated transfer interface and a site/plant-specific refill requirement. Existing citrus-drone evidence concerns canopy spray deposition and cannot validate reservoir filling. Capacity, refill volume, daily release and litres per plant per event must remain distinct. Further research describes an accessible Irrigasc cup and a proposed indoor filling funnel, but still supplies no measured autonomous capture performance for these outdoor reservoirs. Manufacturer RTK hover accuracy concerns aircraft position; it does not measure the volume accepted by an opening. Separate filling from release through a wick, porous wall or soil conduit.
